title: Production inference decision framework — one-pager
content:
Purpose
This is a working one-pager for GTM and field teams that reframes how product and platform buyers make production inference decisions. Use as a short internal brief, field play checklist, and reference for messaging tests. Not polished marketing collateral — intentionally practical and checkout-ready.

Quick summary (two lines)
Engineering teams choose Redwood when they need predictable user experience, controllable cost, and an ops surface that scales with uncertainty. The buying decision is driven less by single-model quality and more by operational risk, unit economics, and time-to-stable-launch.

Why this framework matters (context)
- We see consistent buyer behavior across SMB -> enterprise: initial experiments favor breadth of model access, while production decisions hinge on serving economics and reliability.
- Competing only on model quality is a losing game (models evolve rapidly). The durable differentiation is the inference layer: latency consistency, fallback policies, and transparent cost controls.

Core thesis (more than a slogan)
Teams choose an inference platform when it reduces three uncertainties: 1) Will the system meet latency & availability SLAs under real load? 2) Can we predict and control per-request cost as traffic grows? 3) Will quality regressions be detected and rolled back without customer impact? Redwood solves the decision problem by converting those uncertainties into measurable, auditable controls.

Decision criteria we hear from buyers (evaluation checklist)
- Latency envelope: 95/99th latency under expected load and tail behavior during spikes
- Cost predictability: committed throughput options, tooling to estimate token cost per route, and visibility into batching/cache effects
- Failure modes & fallbacks: automated fallbacks to cheaper model variants or regions with minimal client-side changes
- Data isolation & compliance: VPC/private control plane, KMS integration, audit trails
- Operational telemetry: per-route tracing, token-level cost breakdown, alerting tied to prompt sets
- Rollout controls: canary/A-B routing, automatic rollback, model pinning per-route
- Engineering experience: simple API/SDK, clear upgrade path, reproducible performance benchmarks

How Redwood maps to buyer criteria (core value pillars)
- Predictable performance: runtime-level scheduling + continuous batching keeps 95/99 tails bounded. Engineers get a single SLO view rather than ad-hoc model black boxes.
- Economic transparency: token cost attribution, batch-aware pricing signals, and Optimize recommendations shrink per-token waste.
- Resilience-first design: smart routing + automated fallback policies keep applications online even when a preferred model or region is degraded.
- Unified experience across deployment modes: same API and rollout primitives whether hosted, dedicated, or private — reduces rework when moving to production.
- Ops ergonomics: per-route tracing, prompt-set linked alerts, and prebuilt regressions checks accelerate ops maturity for teams without a large infra org.

Buyer signals / triggers (when to reach out)
- Suddenly variable latency or cost spikes on existing LLM endpoints
- Teams approaching 1M+ tokens/day or building real-time user experiences (chat, recommendation)
- Security/compliance gating (SOC2, ISO, regional data residency) for production rollout
- Disruption from model churn: frequent model swaps and need to automate rollbacks

One-liners for different audiences
- For engineers: "Ship consistent LLM features: same API, predictable latency, and fail-safe routing across hosted and private deployments."
- For platform leads: "Standardize inference across teams with an operations surface that enforces SLAs and makes cost visible at token granularity."
- For product leaders: "Reduce launch risk: avoid surprise latency or costs when experiments scale to real users."

Tactical messaging bullets (field-ready)
- "Keep your UX fast: 95/99 latency SLOs and automated fallbacks if a model slows down."
- "Know your unit cost: token-level cost reports and Optimize recommendations that drive savings without manual tuning."
- "Move from spike-prone to predictable: dedicated capacity and autoscale policies that respect SLAs."

Competitor positioning notes & quick rebuttals (brief)
- Managed cloud AI providers: compete on model inventory but lack refined runtime controls. Rebuttal: emphasize runtime-first features, per-route SLOs, and auditing across deployments.
- Single-vendor model APIs: they own models + API which simplifies small dev flows but causes migration lock-in and opaque performance. Rebuttal: focus on portability, rollback controls, and transparent costs.
- Open-source runtimes/self-host: cheaper at extremes but require ops lift and expertise to achieve consistent tail latency. Rebuttal: highlight our prebuilt kernels, batching infrastructure, and production playbooks.

Open questions / risky assertions to validate
- Does "token-level cost attribution" resonate with PMs or is it an engineer-only metric? (A/B test pitch)
- Are buyers more sensitive to 99th percentile latency or to cost spikes? (collect field data)
- Is the unified API story persuasive enough to overcome early-stage teams' inertia with native managed APIs?

Suggested field experiments (quick A/B ideas)
- Two micro-landing pages: one emphasizing "cost transparency" vs one emphasizing "latency SLOs"; track demo requests and MQLs by org size.
- Sales rebuttal playbook doc: include 3 short scripts (SaaS startup, platform team, enterprise security lead) and record win/loss reasons.
- One-pager for engineering onboarding: short checklist to migrate a single route to Redwood (expected dev time, caveats).

Sample objection handling (cheat-sheet)
- "Why not keep building on top of hosted model APIs?" -> "Hosted model APIs hide variability in latency/cost and don’t offer operational rollouts; Redwood gives you control without the full ops burden."
- "We already self-host inference." -> "Great — Redwood’s runtime and rollout tooling are designed to reduce the 6–12 month ops treadmill for reproducible tail performance; many customers run hybrid deployments."

Next steps (actions for GTM)
- Finalize A/B landing pages with product marketing by 2025-03-22.
- Create a 1-pager migration checklist for solutions engineering by 2025-04-05.
- Run two sales skates to capture buyer signal data and update objections list by end of Q2.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Add a short case study snippet showing cost drop from batching/cache for a mid-market customer. (ask E. Park for numbers)
- Draft an engineer-facing benchmark repo with scripts to reproduce latency envelopes. (SRE / serving-runtime owners)

End of brief.

---
Metadata footnote: this doc is intentionally iterative. Pull quotes and one-liners are meant for quick reuse but verify with A/B before web copy.
